Futurism normally locates the tribulation and Antichrist just before Christ's return, which fits poorly with a long golden age. Some 'latter-day glory' postmillennialists treat Revelation 20 as a still-future era within this age, which is futurist about the millennium itself, but a thoroughgoing futurist reading of Revelation 4–19 with postmillennialism is rare.

Some postmillennialists read Revelation symbolically as the conflict and triumph of Christ's kingdom across the age, drawing their optimism mainly from the Psalms, Prophets and Gospels rather than from a historical decoding of Revelation. B. B. Warfield, for example, read Revelation 19:11-21 as a symbolic picture of the gospel's conquest and Revelation 20:1-6 idealistically (as the intermediate state).

Postmillennialists who combine a preterist reading of the Olivet Discourse and Revelation's judgments with idealist or redemptive-historical readings of other visions (and futurist reading of Revelation 20:7-22:5) are fairly common in practice, though most label themselves partial preterists.

Many amillennialists read the Olivet Discourse (at least Matthew 24:1-34) as fulfilled in AD 70 while expecting a future return, resurrection and judgment. Some read substantial parts of Revelation preteristically too, especially if they date it early (disputed). Jay Adams' 'realized millennialism' joined a largely preterist Revelation to a present millennium.

Because full preterists place the millennium in the past (typically AD 30–70) and deny a future millennium, some describe themselves as 'amillennial' or speak of a 'realized' or 'fulfilled' eschatology, in which the kingdom continues forever after AD 70. Creedal amillennialists reject the pairing, since amillennialism's defining hope is a future return of Christ, one general bodily resurrection and the last judgment, which full preterism denies.

The Reformation pairing: Luther, Calvin and many Reformers kept Augustine's present millennium while reading prophecy historically, identifying the papacy with the Antichrist or man of sin (the original Westminster Confession 25.6 does so). Historically widespread, rare among amillennialists today.

Amillennialists are futurist about the end of the age: many expect a future climactic tribulation, a personal Antichrist and a final apostasy just before Christ returns (2 Thessalonians 2; Revelation 20:7-10), while reading most of Revelation as spanning the whole age. A thoroughgoing futurist reading of Revelation 4–19 is uncommon among amillennialists.

The natural partner of amillennialism: Revelation's cycles portray the whole inter-advent age from different angles (progressive parallelism), symbolising the church's struggle and Christ's victory; Revelation 20 recapitulates the age from the first advent.

Many recent amillennial scholars take a 'modified' or 'eclectic' idealism, recognising first-century referents (Rome, emperor cult), symbolic timeless principles, and a future consummation in the same visions.

Some historic premillennialists see the Olivet Discourse as fulfilled partly in AD 70 and partly at the end, and accept first-century referents for parts of Revelation, while keeping a future tribulation, return and millennium. Thoroughgoing preterism about Revelation 4–19 is rare in this camp.

Incompatible: historic premillennialism requires a future visible return of Christ followed by a future earthly reign, whereas full preterism holds that the Parousia occurred in AD 70 and that the millennium (typically AD 30–70) is already past.

Historically very common: from Joseph Mede (1627) through Isaac Newton and E. B. Elliott's Horae Apocalypticae (1844) and H. Grattan Guinness, premillennialists read Revelation as a sequential history of the church climaxing in Christ's premillennial return. Common before the rise of dispensational futurism; rare today.

The dominant modern pairing: a future tribulation and Antichrist, a posttribulational return, and a millennium afterward, typically with the moderate futurism of Ladd, who also acknowledged first-century referents.

A purely idealist reading treats Revelation's visions as timeless symbols rather than a sequence, which undercuts the chronological reading of Revelation 19–20 on which premillennialism rests. A few interpreters combine idealist readings of the central visions with a premillennial reading of chapters 19–20.
Many evangelical commentators blend preterist (first-century setting), idealist (timeless message) and futurist (consummation) elements while reading Revelation 20 premillennially.

Dispensationalism places the seventieth week of Daniel and Revelation 4–19 in the future, so preterism is generally rejected (Thomas Ice is a leading critic). Some progressive dispensationalists, however, read Luke 21:20-24 as fulfilled in AD 70 while keeping a future tribulation.

Incompatible: dispensationalism requires a future seventieth week, a future rapture and return, and a future millennium for national Israel, while full preterism places all of these, including the millennium (typically AD 30–70), in the first century.

Darby and later dispensationalists rejected historicism in favour of futurism. The one common exception is the reading of the seven churches of Revelation 2–3 as seven successive eras of church history (popularised by the Scofield notes), a historicist element within an otherwise futurist system.
The defining pairing: Revelation 4–22 and Daniel's seventieth week are future, following the rapture of the church; the millennium is a literal future reign.

Incompatible in its pure form: idealism treats the visions as timeless symbols without concrete future referents, whereas dispensationalism insists on literal, future fulfilment of specific events for Israel and the nations.

Progressive dispensationalists often acknowledge first-century referents and present-age 'already' fulfilments alongside a primarily futurist reading, a moderate eclecticism that traditional dispensationalists resist.

A natural pairing: reading the book 'from victory', with the Rider on the white horse conquering by his word (Revelation 19:11-16) and the harvest as gospel fruit (Revelation 14:14-16), fits a hope that Christ's present reign will increasingly fill the earth. Many proponents also have a preterist-leaning view of AD 70 as the end of the old covenant age.

Equally natural: the thousand years as Christ's present reign and the first resurrection as the new birth follow the Augustinian reading of Revelation 20, and the 'two cities' structure echoes Tyconius and Augustine. Amillennial-leaning proponents are less confident about the outward triumph of the gospel within history.

Uncommon: the view reads the millennium as Christ's present reign and the first resurrection as the new birth, whereas historic premillennialism needs a future earthly reign after a bodily first resurrection. A few readers combine Christ-centred spiritual applications of chapters 1–19 with a premillennial reading of Revelation 20.

Incompatible in substance: the Spiritual Understanding rejects a future seven-year tribulation, a separate pre-tribulation rapture and a distinct national programme for Israel, and reads the church as the Bride and the New Jerusalem. Dispensationalists may draw devotional Christ-centred applications from Revelation, but not as their interpretive method.
The Millennium
When and what is the millennium of Revelation 20?

Revelation 20:1-10 speaks six times of a 'thousand years' during which Satan is bound and the saints reign with Christ. Views divide on whether this period is present or future, whether it comes before or after Christ's return, whether the number is literal or symbolic, and whether the reign is on earth or in heaven.
The whole present age between Christ's two comings (symbolic number)
The present reign of departed saints with Christ in heaven during the gospel age
The present age, in which the gospel progressively triumphs and flowers into a golden age before Christ returns
A future era of gospel triumph within history, still before Christ's return, after Antichrist falls
A future earthly reign of Christ after his return, before the final state
A future, literal 1,000-year Davidic kingdom on earth, fulfilling promises to national Israel
Already fulfilled: the covenantal transition period that ended in AD 70
The Binding of Satan
What is the binding of Satan in Revelation 20:1-3, and when does it happen?

An angel seizes the dragon, binds him for a thousand years and seals the abyss 'so that he might not deceive the nations any longer'. Is this Christ's victory at his first coming (compare Matthew 12:29, John 12:31, Colossians 2:15), a future total imprisonment after his return, or a turning point in church history?
Bound by Christ's first-coming victory: restrained from stopping the gospel among the nations
Bound at the cross and finally crushed by AD 70
Bound at a turning point in church history (e.g. the fall of paganism or of Antichrist)
A future, total imprisonment of Satan after Christ returns
The First Resurrection
What is the 'first resurrection' of Revelation 20:4-6?

Those who 'came to life' reign with Christ for the thousand years; 'the rest of the dead' do not live until the thousand years end. The question is whether the first resurrection is spiritual (new birth, or the soul's entrance into heaven) or bodily, and how it relates to the general resurrection (John 5:24-29, 1 Corinthians 15).
Spiritual: the new birth and union with the risen Christ
Spiritual: believers' souls entering Christ's presence at death and reigning in heaven
Figurative: the revival of the martyrs' cause and spirit in a later era
Covenantal: the raising of God's people from 'death' under the old covenant, completed in AD 70
Bodily resurrection of believers at Christ's return, before the millennium
The Second Coming
What is the Second Coming, and is it past or future, single or in stages?

All historic creeds confess that Christ 'will come again in glory to judge the living and the dead'. Views differ on its relation to the millennium, whether it unfolds in two stages (rapture and glorious appearing), and, for full preterists, whether it was already fulfilled in AD 70.
One future, visible, bodily return that brings the general resurrection, final judgment and new creation together
A future bodily return before the millennium; final judgment follows a thousand years later
Future, in two stages: a pre-tribulational rapture, then the glorious appearing to set up the millennial kingdom
Fulfilled in AD 70 with the judgment on Jerusalem; no future bodily return is expected
The Rapture
When is the church 'caught up' to meet the Lord (1 Thessalonians 4:17)?

Paul says living believers will be 'caught up' (Latin rapiemur) to meet the Lord in the air. Debate centres on whether this is a distinct event that removes the church before a future tribulation, an event within or after that tribulation, simply one aspect of the single Second Coming, or something already fulfilled.
Pre-tribulational: the church is removed before a future seven-year tribulation
Mid-tribulational or pre-wrath: during the tribulation, before God's wrath is poured out
Post-tribulational: at Christ's return after a future tribulation, with the church passing through it
Not a separate event: believers are gathered to meet Christ at his one Second Coming
Fulfilled in the first century, in connection with AD 70
The Great Tribulation
When is the 'great tribulation' (Matthew 24:21, Revelation 7:14)?

Jesus warns of a distress unequalled 'from the beginning of the world until now', tied to the 'abomination of desolation' and flight from Judea. Is it the Jewish War of AD 66-70, an experience spread through church history, a final future crisis, or a future seven-year period?
Fulfilled in the Jewish War and the fall of Jerusalem, AD 66-70
Spread through church history (e.g. 1,260 years of persecution read by the day-year principle)
Throughout the age (with AD 70 as an anticipation), intensifying into a final tribulation before Christ returns
A future, final tribulation that the church passes through before Christ returns
A future seven-year period: Daniel's seventieth week
Antichrist and the Beast
Who is the Antichrist, the 'man of lawlessness' and the beast?

John speaks of 'many antichrists' (1 John 2:18), Paul of a 'man of lawlessness' (2 Thessalonians 2:3-12) and Revelation of a beast numbered 666 (Revelation 13:18). Are these first-century figures such as Nero, a historical institution such as the papacy, a recurring anti-Christian principle, or a future world ruler?
A first-century figure: Nero as the beast; the man of lawlessness tied to AD 70
The papacy as a historical institution (with Islam often in view elsewhere in Revelation)
A recurring anti-Christian principle, likely culminating in a final personal Antichrist
A recurring anti-Christian power (persecuting state and false religion) in every age
A future individual world ruler during the coming tribulation
'This Generation'
What does 'this generation will not pass away' mean (Matthew 24:34)?

Jesus says 'this generation' (Greek he genea haute) will not pass until 'all these things' happen. Does it mean his contemporaries (and if so, is everything in the discourse fulfilled by AD 70?), the generation alive when the end-time signs appear, or the Jewish people or an evil kind of people?
Jesus' contemporaries: everything in the discourse, including his coming, was fulfilled by AD 70
Jesus' contemporaries: the signs and judgment of verses 4-34 were fulfilled by AD 70; the final coming is still future
Jesus' contemporaries saw the temple fall, but the discourse blends AD 70 with the end of the age
The future generation that sees the end-time signs
The Jewish people, or an evil 'kind' of people, which will last until the end
Daniel's Seventy Weeks
When is the seventieth week of Daniel 9:24-27 fulfilled, and does a gap separate it from the first sixty-nine?

Gabriel's prophecy of 'seventy sevens' (Daniel 9:24-27) sets out six goals: finishing transgression, atoning for iniquity, bringing in everlasting righteousness, sealing vision and prophet, and anointing a most holy place. It also says an 'anointed one' will be cut off after sixty-nine weeks. Interpreters disagree on whether the seventieth week runs on straight after the sixty-ninth and is fulfilled in Christ's first coming and its sequel in AD 70, or whether an interval (the church age) separates it so that it remains a future seven-year period. They also disagree on whether 'he' who confirms a covenant in Daniel 9:27 is the Messiah or a future prince, and on how literally to count the numbers.
Continuous: the 70th week is fulfilled in Christ's ministry, death and the new covenant, with AD 70 as its consequence
Continuous: the seventy weeks run up to and end in the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70, completing all prophecy
Symbolic and Christ-centred: the 70th week begins with Christ, and its second half spans the church age to his return
Gap: a parenthesis (the church age) follows week 69, and the 70th week is a future seven-year tribulation
Future final week tied to the Antichrist, without a full dispensational Israel/church parenthesis
Date of Revelation
When was the book of Revelation written: before AD 70 under Nero, or c. AD 95 under Domitian?

Disputed. The late date (c. AD 95-96, late in Domitian's reign) rests mainly on Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.30.3), followed by Eusebius and most later tradition, together with internal hints such as the condition of the seven churches and possible echoes of the Nero-redivivus legend. The early date (c. AD 65-68, under Nero or just after) appeals to the measuring of a still-standing temple (Revelation 11:1-2), the 'seventh king' count (Revelation 17:9-11), the possible Nero gematria of 666 (Revelation 13:18), the time texts (Revelation 1:1, 1:3, 22:10), and a rereading of Irenaeus's ambiguous sentence. Most modern commentators favour the late date, but a significant minority, including some non-preterists such as J. A. T. Robinson, argue for an early one. The question matters most for preterist readings, which need a pre-70 date if Revelation predicts Jerusalem's fall.
Early date: written before AD 70, usually c. 65-68 under Nero
Late date: written c. AD 95-96 under Domitian
Date secondary: the interpretation does not depend on it (adherents differ, most leaning late)
Israel and the Church
Does ethnic Israel have a distinct future in God's plan, and what does 'all Israel will be saved' (Romans 11:26) mean?

Everyone agrees that Romans 9-11 is central. The questions are whether 'all Israel' means a future large-scale conversion of ethnic Jews, the full number of elect Jews saved throughout history, or the whole church of Jews and Gentiles. A further question is whether the Old Testament land and kingdom promises await a literal national fulfilment (dispensationalism) or are fulfilled and expanded in Christ and the new creation (covenant and progressive covenantal views). Holding a future conversion of Jews is not the same as holding a distinct national programme: many postmillennialists and some amillennialists expect the first without the second.
Future large-scale conversion of ethnic Jews into the one church (Romans 11:25-26), with no separate national programme
Israel and the church are distinct: a future national salvation, return to the land and central role in the millennial kingdom
'All Israel' is the full number of elect Jews saved throughout the church age, not a future national event
'All Israel' is the whole people of God, Jew and Gentile, united in the Messiah
Israel's promised salvation and restoration were completed in the first-century remnant and the new-covenant consummation of AD 70
Historical Optimism
What should the church expect of history before Christ returns: gospel triumph, mixed growth of good and evil, or decline into apostasy?

This is the practical, 'mood' question of eschatology. Postmillennialists expect the Great Commission to succeed in history, so that most of the world is discipled before the Second Coming. Amillennialists usually describe themselves as neither optimistic nor pessimistic about history. Wheat and tares grow together, the kingdom advances alongside persistent evil, and a final intensification precedes the end. Their optimism rests on Christ's return. Premillennialists expect apostasy and tribulation before the return, with the world's restoration coming through Christ's personal reign. Every view is hopeful about the final outcome. They differ on what happens before it.
Optimistic: the gospel will prevail and disciple the nations before Christ returns
Optimistic without a terminus: the kingdom, fully come, grows without end and history has no final consummation
'Realistic': kingdom and evil grow side by side until the end, with hope fixed on the return
Decline: apostasy and tribulation precede the return, and Christ himself restores the world in the millennium
Decline and rescue: the church age ends in apostasy, the church is raptured and the world enters tribulation
The Kingdom of God
In what sense is the kingdom of God present now, and what form does its future take?

Almost everyone now accepts an 'already/not yet' kingdom inaugurated by Jesus. The questions are what form the 'already' takes and how much of the 'not yet' falls within history. Postmillennialists stress progressive expansion of Christ's present reign until it fills the earth (Daniel 2:35, Matthew 13:31-33). Amillennialists stress a present spiritual reign of Christ and the saints, consummated in the new heavens and new earth. Premillennialists add a future earthly kingdom between the Second Coming and the eternal state. Classic dispensationalists see the Davidic kingdom as offered, rejected and postponed. Full preterists hold that the kingdom arrived in its fullness in AD 70.
Inaugurated and progressively expanding: Christ reigns now from heaven and his kingdom grows to fill the earth before his return
Already/not yet: a present spiritual reign, consummated at the return in the new heavens and earth
Inaugurated now, with a future earthly millennial phase after the return and before the eternal state
Davidic kingdom offered, rejected and postponed, to be established literally on earth for a thousand years
Fully come: the kingdom was consummated in AD 70 and is eternal and ever-present, with no future consummation
The Final Judgment
Is there one general resurrection and judgment of all people at Christ's return, or several judgments separated in time?

The historic creeds confess that Christ 'will come again to judge the living and the dead'. Reformed confessions (Westminster Confession 32-33) teach one general resurrection of just and unjust followed by one general judgment (John 5:28-29, Acts 24:15, Matthew 25:31-46). Premillennialists separate the resurrection of the righteous at the return from that of the wicked after the thousand years (Revelation 20:4-6, 11-15). Dispensationalists further distinguish the judgment seat of Christ for believers, the judgment of living nations and Israel, and the Great White Throne. Full preterists place the resurrection and judgment at AD 70 and treat individual judgment as ongoing at death. Critics regard this as a departure from creedal orthodoxy.
One general resurrection and judgment of the righteous and the wicked at Christ's return
Two resurrections a thousand years apart: the righteous at the return, the wicked before the Great White Throne
Several distinct judgments: believers' rewards (bema), living nations and Israel, and the Great White Throne
Judgment and resurrection fulfilled at AD 70, with individuals judged at death ever since
Place in Church History
Where does each view's historical weight lie: in which era did it arise, dominate or flourish?

Every school claims historical roots, and each claim is debated. Early chiliasm (Papias, Justin, Irenaeus) is the strongest patristic witness for premillennialism. Augustine's reading of Revelation 20 (City of God XX) shaped the medieval and Reformation churches. Protestant historicism dominated from the Reformation to the mid-nineteenth century. Postmillennial hope flourished among Puritans, in the Great Awakening and at Old Princeton. Dispensationalism arose with J. N. Darby in the 1830s and spread through the Scofield Reference Bible. Systematic preterism and futurism both have early-modern origins, often linked to the Jesuits Alcázar and Ribera, and both have recent revivals. Antiquity is not proof, and proponents of newer views argue that they are recovering biblical teaching rather than inventing it.
Patristic roots: strongest in the second-century fathers (Papias, Justin, Irenaeus)
Patristic seeds, systematised in the Counter-Reformation and revived in the nineteenth century
Augustinian-dominant: the majority view from Augustine through the Middle Ages and the Reformation
Reformation-dominant: the standard Protestant reading from the Reformers to the mid-nineteenth century
Puritan flourishing: rose in the seventeenth century and dominated through the Awakenings and Old Princeton
Nineteenth-century rise: from Darby (1830s) and the Scofield Bible to twentieth-century evangelical dominance
Patristic AD 70 readings, systematised in the seventeenth century and revived since the 1980s
Recent: a nineteenth-century precursor (J. S. Russell) and a movement since the 1970s
Modern scholarly synthesis: a late twentieth-century blend drawing on every older stream

The thousand years is a symbolic number for the long era between Christ's enthronement and his return. During it the mediatorial King rules from heaven, and through the Spirit-blessed preaching of the gospel the nations are gradually discipled, until the world as a whole is Christianised. Christ returns after this age of gospel prosperity, so his coming is 'post' millennial.

Postmillennialists differ over whether the millennium is the whole inter-advent age (Gentry, Mathison) or a future 'golden age' that dawns later within it (Jonathan Edwards and many Puritans). Warfield identified Revelation 20:4-6 with the heavenly state of the saints while still expecting earthly gospel triumph.

Revelation 20 recapitulates the whole church age rather than following Revelation 19 in time. The 'thousand years' symbolises the complete period from Christ's resurrection and ascension to his return, during which Satan is bound and believers reign with Christ. Some amillennialists, following Jay Adams and Anthony Hoekema, prefer the label 'realised millennialism': there is a millennium, but it is now, not a future earthly era.
Amillennialists differ on whether the reign of Revelation 20:4 is mainly the heavenly reign of departed saints (Hoekema, Riddlebarger) or the believer's present spiritual life (Augustine).

Revelation 19:11-21 and 20:1-10 form one sequence: Christ returns, the beast is destroyed, Satan is bound, and the saints are raised to reign with Christ on the earth before the final judgment. The millennium is a real stage of God's kingdom in history, though not centred on a restored national theocracy. Many historic premillennialists hold the number may be symbolic of a long period.
Early chiliasts such as Justin Martyr and Irenaeus pictured an earthly reign centred on a rebuilt Jerusalem; modern historic premillennialists (Ladd, Blomberg) are more reserved about its details.

After the tribulation, Christ returns to establish a literal thousand-year kingdom on earth, reigning from Jerusalem on David's throne. The kingdom fulfils, in their plain sense, God's unconditional covenant promises to national Israel of land, seed and throne, with redeemed Gentiles sharing in its blessings. It is a real earthly theocracy that ends with Satan's final revolt and the great white throne judgment.
Progressive dispensationalists (Blaising, Bock) see the Davidic kingdom as already inaugurated at Christ's ascension, with the earthly millennium as its future stage.

Most partial preterists read Revelation 4-19 as fulfilled in the judgments of the AD 60s, so Revelation 20 describes the era that follows Christ's first-century victory. The thousand years is the present church age in which Christ reigns and the gospel advances. Most partial preterists are postmillennial, but the approach itself only requires that the millennium is not a future era after a future tribulation.

Gentry, DeMar and Bahnsen pair preterism with postmillennialism; Jay Adams and some others pair it with amillennialism (stance present-church-age). Preterism is a hermeneutic for Revelation's timing, not a millennial view in itself.

Most full preterists hold that the millennium was the transition era between Christ's first coming and his return in AD 70, often reckoned as the forty years from the cross to the fall of Jerusalem. During it the old covenant age was passing away and the new covenant kingdom was being established. With the judgment, resurrection and parousia complete by AD 70, believers now live in the eternal new-covenant age pictured by the new heavens and earth.

Some full preterists instead treat the thousand years as the unending new-covenant age after AD 70. Critics note that this reading requires a past general resurrection and final judgment, which places it outside historic creedal orthodoxy.

Historicists read Revelation as a continuous prophecy of church history, so Revelation 20 comes after the fall of the papal Antichrist and the Turkish woes. For the Puritan and Edwardsean tradition this is a coming golden age of worldwide revival, the conversion of the Jews and gospel triumph, still before Christ returns. Many nineteenth-century historicists instead placed Christ's personal return before it.

Historicists are split: Edwards and most Puritans were postmillennial, while E. B. Elliott, H. Grattan Guinness and others were premillennial (closer to future-earthly-reign). Some older historicists dated the thousand years from Constantine.

Futurists read Revelation 4-22 as still to come, so Revelation 20 follows Christ's return in Revelation 19 in sequence. The thousand years is therefore a future reign of Christ on earth after he defeats the beast. Most futurists take the number literally and expect the reign to fulfil Old Testament kingdom prophecies.
Most futurists are dispensational (stance future-davidic-kingdom); historic premillennialists such as Ladd are futurist without Israel-centred dispensational distinctives.

Idealists read Revelation's visions as symbolic portraits of the conflict between Christ and evil repeated across the whole age. Revelation 20 shows the same period from heaven's side: the martyrs and faithful dead are already reigning with Christ while the church suffers on earth. The thousand years is the complete gospel age, not a datable period.
Idealism is usually paired with amillennialism (Hendriksen, Milligan), but as a hermeneutic it does not strictly settle the millennial question.

Eclectic interpreters such as G. K. Beale combine a first-century setting, a symbolic transhistorical meaning, and a future consummation. Beale reads Revelation 20 as recapitulating the church age: the thousand years symbolises the inter-advent period in which the deceased saints reign with Christ. Other eclectics weigh the sequence of Revelation 19-20 differently.
Beale's 'redemptive-historical idealism' is amillennial, while Grant Osborne's eclectic commentary is premillennial (future-earthly-reign).

Christ bound the strong man at his first coming, through his ministry, death, resurrection and ascension. Satan's binding is specific: he can no longer deceive the nations or stop the gospel from discipling them. This restraint is what makes the progressive worldwide triumph of the gospel possible.

The binding is Christ's victory over the devil during his messianic mission, applied throughout the church age. Satan is not inactive, but he can no longer keep the nations in darkness or stop the gospel going out to them. Revelation 20:3 echoes Jesus' parable of binding the strong man and his statement that the ruler of this world is cast out.
